name: RUNX1 familial platelet disorder with myeloid malignancy
aliases: familial platelet disorder with predisposition to acute myeloid leukaemia

clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant disorder caused by germline mutations in RUNX1, characterised by lifelong mild-to-moderate thrombocytopenia and a substantial lifetime risk of myeloid malignancy
Platelet counts are usually only modestly reduced, so the bleeding tendency is often disproportionate to the count because of an accompanying qualitative platelet defect
Platelet aggregation studies frequently show a dense-granule (delta storage pool) defect with impaired responses to collagen and adrenaline
A family history of unexplained thrombocytopenia, easy bruising, or leukaemia across generations should prompt consideration of a germline RUNX1 lesion
Reported lifetime risk of progression to myelodysplasia or acute myeloid leukaemia is high, commonly cited around a third to a half of carriers
Somatic second hits (for example a second RUNX1 allele, or acquired mutations in genes such as CDC25C, GATA2 or the acquisition of trisomy 21 in marrow) often accompany transformation
Diagnosis rests on germline genetic testing, ideally on non-haematopoietic tissue such as cultured skin fibroblasts to avoid contamination by clonal blood cells
Because the mutation is germ line, related potential stem-cell donors must be screened to avoid transplanting an affected graft
reference.pathophysiology: RUNX1 encodes the alpha subunit of the core-binding factor transcription complex, a master regulator of definitive haematopoiesis and megakaryocyte maturation. Germline loss-of-function or dominant-negative mutations reduce functional RUNX1 dosage (haploinsufficiency) and disturb the transcriptional programme that drives platelet production and granule formation, producing both a low platelet count and defective platelet function. The impaired transcriptional network also destabilises the myeloid compartment, so affected stem cells are primed for clonal evolution; acquisition of additional somatic mutations over time drives progression to myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukaemia.
additionalDifferentials: MYH9-related disorder and other inherited macrothrombocytopenias
Storage pool disease and other qualitative platelet disorders
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with review of the peripheral blood film for platelet number and morphology
Platelet aggregometry and dense-granule (delta storage pool) assessment
Germline RUNX1 sequencing performed on cultured fibroblasts or another non-haematopoietic source
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics for baseline and surveillance
Serial monitoring for acquired clonal mutations and karyotypic change
Screening of related potential haematopoietic stem-cell donors
redFlags: New or worsening cytopenias, monocytosis, or circulating blasts suggesting transformation to myelodysplasia or leukaemia
Emergence of a new clonal cytogenetic abnormality on marrow surveillance
Rapidly falling platelet count or unexplained systemic symptoms
Bleeding out of proportion to the platelet count indicating a significant qualitative defect
reference.prognosis: The bleeding tendency is usually manageable, but the defining concern is the high lifetime risk of myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukaemia; outcomes depend on early detection through surveillance and on timely allogeneic transplantation using a mutation-negative donor when transformation supervenes.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the condition as chronic immune thrombocytopenia and exposing patients to unnecessary immunosuppression or splenectomy
Testing only blood-derived DNA, which can miss or misattribute the germline variant when a blood clone is present
Using an affected relative as a stem-cell donor because germline status was not checked
Underestimating bleeding risk by relying on the platelet count alone rather than assessing platelet function
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Managing the bleeding tendency with antifibrinolytics such as tranexamic acid and platelet transfusion for significant bleeding or surgery, while avoiding antiplatelet agents such as aspirin and NSAIDs
Considering desmopressin to improve platelet function around haemostatic challenges
Regular haematological surveillance with serial full blood counts and periodic bone marrow examination and cytogenetics to detect progression to myelodysplasia or acute myeloid leukaemia
Monitoring for acquired clonal mutations and karyotypic change that herald transformation
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation when myelodysplasia or acute leukaemia supervenes
Screening related potential stem-cell donors to ensure a mutation-negative graft
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance, with germline RUNX1 testing performed on a non-haematopoietic source such as cultured fibroblasts
